Chapter: commons/maps/FormFinding_Catenary/final.md:15.

Encounter in the text: Three washing lines pegged with towels and shirts, supported at their ends by crossbars. These curves are sampled from cosh. Their sag comes from three chosen parameters; the washing adds colour and an association with weight, but it adds no load to the calculation. Then look up. Above each line hangs its ghost: the same curve mirrored upward as a pale arch. The cathedral is implied.

coins.name: Watch one sphere, then the wave
coins.reflection:
Chapter: commons/maps/WaveFunctions_3D_Wave_Propagation/final.md:3.

Encounter in the text: Choose one sphere near the centre of the lattice. Follow that sphere alone. It rises and returns, keeping its place in the grid. Now widen your attention. Something has travelled beyond the place you were watching.

Critical reading: commons/maps/WaveFunctions_3D_Wave_Propagation/critical.md.

Critical text to review (may describe an earlier layout): A wave leaves a source and spreads. The energy packed into the first wavefront is the same energy spread over a larger sphere one second later, so the amplitude at any given point drops as the square of the distance. This is the inverse-square law, and it is the first thing the map makes physical: the field is bright near the emitter and fades…

Suggested invitation and song direction. Review the current encounter before choosing approach/after-action timing; no new recording or runtime trigger is created here.

coins.reflection:
Chapter: commons/maps/Wavefunctions_Bernini/final.md:5.

Encounter in the text: Choose one ridge on a twisting shaft and follow it upward. Notice how it moves around the vertical axis as height increases. Change your viewpoint and find the ridge again. Then compare it with a neighbouring column.

Critical reading: commons/maps/Wavefunctions_Bernini/critical.md.

Critical text to review (may describe an earlier layout): Baroque architecture was accused of excess. Its critics called it overwrought, undisciplined, a break with classical restraint. Bernini's solomonic columns — the twisting spirals that support the Baldachin at Saint Peter's — were the most-accused examples of this excess. They did not behave like columns. They wavered. They turned as they rose.…

coins.reflection:
Chapter: commons/maps/WaveFunctions_John_Cage/final.md:7.

Encounter in the text: Let the soundscape load. A continuous layer stays with you; other sounds enter and leave. Count a few entrances without trying to force them into a regular beat. Then listen to the intervals instead. An interval can become the part you are waiting for.

Critical reading: commons/maps/WaveFunctions_John_Cage/critical.md.

Critical text to review (may describe an earlier layout): Cage's 4'33" tells the performer to play nothing. What the audience hears is not nothing. They hear coughs, ventilation, traffic, the creak of chairs, the rustle of programmes. The piece claims these as the composition. It reframes the attention as the event and the performed absence as the occasion.

Chapter: commons/maps/WaveFunctions_AirMusic/final.md:7.

Critical text to review (may describe an earlier layout): Steven Feld writes about acoustemology: sound as a way of knowing, and knowing-through-sound as inseparable from the place the sound is made in. This hall is a small place of that kind. It is built round a void, and the thing you come to know in it is the difference between an event and its continuation.

Chapter: commons/maps/Random_Space_Geometry/final.md:5.

coins.name: Look at what the column carries
coins.floor_title: Noise Columns / what keeps a body changing?
coins.reflection:
Chapter: commons/maps/Noise_Columns/final.md:5.

Encounter in the text: Three marble columns stand in the east half of the room. Their shafts come from the same recipe, at the same resolution. The plates at their feet say nothing yet. The little instrument between the silhouettes offers ways to look; it leaves the names until you ask. Stand where you can see all three at once and watch for a while before you press anything.

Critical reading: commons/maps/Noise_Columns/critical.md.

Critical text to review (may describe an earlier layout): Recognizing a column brings an expectation of support. These columns carry that expectation into a scene where they hold nothing up. Their simulation concerns appearance and generated geometry. The discrepancy can be an encounter in its own right: what makes us read a body as architecture before asking what it can carry?

Suggested invitation and song direction. Review the current encounter before choosing approach/after-action timing; no new recording or runtime trigger is created here.

coins.name: Compare the two receivers
coins.reflection:
Chapter: commons/maps/Noise_One/final.md:3.

Encounter in the text: Two rings stand upright on a bench. There is room to stop and see both before moving closer. One wears its variation as small folds. The other keeps a round outline while colour travels across it. The columns behind us asked where change enters a body. Here the question becomes more intimate: could these two surfaces be receiving the same thing?

Critical reading: commons/maps/Noise_One/critical.md.

Critical text to review (may describe an earlier layout): The torus comparison begins with a practical loss. Negative samples move the relief inward but, under the first colour rule, all become black. Different numbers arrive at one appearance. The shader has computed their difference; a later operation has refused to distinguish it.

Suggested invitation and song direction. Review the current encounter before choosing approach/after-action timing; no new recording or runtime trigger is created here.

Both changes keep a history that the visible boundary alone does not disclose.

Walk its edge first. Does the opening meet the floor, or does…

Its ring can look like an invitation while its sampled field leaves a gap above the floor, a constriction behind the first view or a collision surface facing the wrong way. “Portal” names an intention; the field and the body decide what arrives.

Chapter: commons/maps/Russell_Paradox/final.md:9.

Encounter in the text: The workbench begins at cell 5. Its rule reads: collect all sets that are not members of themselves. Call the result R. Does R belong to R?

Critical reading: commons/maps/Russell_Paradox/critical.md.

Critical text to review (may describe an earlier layout): NonEuclidean_Spaces showed that axioms are choices. Russell's paradox shows that some choices eat themselves. The set of all sets that don't contain themselves is not a trick question. It is a legitimate construction within naive set theory, formed by the same rules that form every other set. The rules produce it. The rules cannot survive it.

Chapter: commons/maps/Godel_Incompleteness/final.md:7.

The floor has already decided, in capitals, from EVERY FORMAL SYSTEM to SELF-REFERENCE IS THE EDGE; walk over its verdict and ask the same question of the machine. Critical text to review (may describe an earlier layout): Russell's paradox was explosive — a contradiction that destroyed naive set theory from the inside. Godel's incompleteness is colder, more permanent. The system does not break. The walls hold. The axioms are consistent. And precisely because they hold, something escapes. Consistency is not the achievement the formalists hoped it would be.…
